messages:
maria-support: Hi @john-cust-devops — I see your private deployment is failing to reach our control plane for token refreshes. Can you paste the error you see from your side?
john-cust-devops: getting `curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer` from the healthcheck to https://controlplane.redwood.example.com/v1/ping — happens intermittently but mostly fails. Only outbound 443 allowed on SG/NACL currently.
maria-support: thanks. quick ask: can you run a l4 connect test and a tcpdump while reproducing? e.g. `nc -vz controlplane.redwood.example.com 443` and `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host controlplane.redwood.example.com and port 443 -w out.pcap`
john-cust-devops: ran `nc -vz` — result: `connect to 34.216.XX.XX port 443 (tcp) failed: Connection reset by peer`
priya-netops: that pattern usually means an outbound SYN went out but the return path was blocked (NACL is stateless). If you're only allowing outbound port 443 on the NACL but not allowing the ephemeral ports back in, the control plane's SYN-ACK will be dropped. NACLs must allow ephemeral range for return traffic.
dan-eng-infra: to add: Security Groups are stateful so if SG allows outbound 443 you may be fine there; NACL must explicitly allow ephemeral ephemeral ranges both outbound (if you restrict) and inbound for the replies. What does your NACL egress/inbound look like?
john-cust-devops: here's current NACL snippet (we restrict a lot):
```
Inbound: ALLOW 443 0.0.0.0/0 (rule 100)
Inbound: DENY ALL (rule 32767)
Outbound: ALLOW 443 0.0.0.0/0 (rule 100)
Outbound: DENY ALL (rule 32767)
```
priya-netops: yep that's the issue — since NACLs are stateless you need to allow ephemeral return ports. Recommend adding:
Outbound: ALLOW 1024-65535 0.0.0.0/0 (rule 110)
Inbound: ALLOW 1024-65535 0.0.0.0/0 (rule 110)
Or narrower: 32768-61000 if you prefer the OS ephemeral range. Also ensure the rule order (lower number => evaluated first).
maria-support: also note that if there's a corporate firewall or IDS doing TLS inspection it can reset connections. If you see a TCP RST from a middlebox in `tcpdump`, paste the pcap/syn/ack details.
john-cust-devops: ran tcpdump; here's a short extract:
```
12:03:10.123456 IP 10.0.2.12.51234 > 34.216.XX.XX.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240
12:03:10.234567 IP 34.216.XX.XX.443 > 10.0.2.12.51234: RST, seq 0, win 0
```
priya-netops: RST from our control plane IP suggests the SYN reached them but they reset. That can happen if they see a missing return route or a security policy on their side. However more commonly with cloud NACLs you see the reply dropped (no SYN-ACK). The RST here could be because the control plane got a SYN out-of-window (rare) or because of explicit deny. Can you confirm you don't have a NAT gateway or proxy that's rewriting source ports?
john-cust-devops: we go through a NAT gateway using a managed egress NAT; source ports look like high ports (51234) when I inspect logs.
dan-eng-infra: ok two plausible paths: 1) middlebox on customer side is sending RST (maybe an inline IPS) 2) our control plane is actively resetting because of an unexpected TLS client hello (rare). Can you run `sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -A port 443 and host 34.216.XX.XX` and share the packet capture? If you can't share pcap, check whether the RST originates from the NAT IP or from 34.216.XX.XX.
john-cust-devops: confirmed RST source IP is 34.216.XX.XX (control plane).
priya-netops: hmm. In that case, likely their control plane sees a TCP handshake but then sends RST because session didn't match expected flow — often due to asymmetric routing/backwards NAT. Double-check our egress ACLs and ensure we allow the ephemeral range. Also ask Redwood to whitelist the NAT egress IP on their side?
maria-support: we've validated that our control plane will accept connections from any ephemeral client ports but we do maintain an allowlist for customer egress NAT IPs for private plans. Can you paste the public NAT IP?
john-cust-devops: NAT IP is 54.210.77.211
maria-support: thanks — I added 54.210.77.211 to the customer allowlist and also asked infra to monitor for resets. Priya, can you advise the exact NACL entries John should add so it's reproducible?
priya-netops: sure — run these aws CLI commands (example):
```
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry 
  --network-acl-id acl-abcdef12 
  --rule-number 110 
  --protocol "-1" 
  --rule-action allow 
  --egress 
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535

aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry 
  --network-acl-id acl-abcdef12 
  --rule-number 110 
  --protocol "-1" 
  --rule-action allow 
  --ingress 
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535
```
Adjust port-range to your OS ephemeral range if needed. Verify rule numbers are lower than the DENY ALL (32767).
john-cust-devops: added ephemeral allow rules and retried. `nc -vz` now returns: `Connection to 34.216.XX.XX 443 port [tcp/*] succeeded!`
maria-support: great! can you also confirm the API healthchecks are green and the token refreshes completed?
john-cust-devops: healthchecks are green, no more 56 errors. Thanks team.
priya-netops: wrapping up: doc note for others — when using NACLs, remember they're stateless: allow both outbound 443 and the ephemeral port range for return traffic, or rely on SG statefulness. Also consider locking to specific control plane IPs if you need tight egress controls.
dan-eng-infra: filed a quick KB entry for private customers with NAT + NACL guidance and ephemeral ranges.
maria-support: closing thread — re-open if it reappears :thumbsup:
